rows: Detect the dominant language of each text (ISO-639 code, fastText lid.176)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Identify the dominant natural language of each input string and return its two-letter ISO-639-1 code (`en`, `fr`, `de`, `es`, ...), using the fastText `lid.176` model.

**When to use:** routing mixed-language corpora, filtering a table down to one language before applying English-only models (e.g. VADER sentiment), or building a language histogram with `GROUP BY`.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` ISO-639 code. NULL or empty input yields NULL. Very short or ambiguous strings can be misclassified -- pair with `detect_lang_conf` and threshold on confidence when accuracy matters.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang

Returns the ISO-639-1 language code of each text value, computed with the fastText `lid.176` identifier -- for example `fr` for `Bonjour le monde` and `en` for a plain English sentence.

Use it to segment a multilingual column before language-specific processing. Combine with `nlp.detect_lang_conf` to discard low-confidence guesses; very short snippets are inherently hard to classify.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Identify the language of a literal string", "sql": "SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS lang"}]
rows.vgi.title: Detect Language Code

rows: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS lang
Confidence (0-1) of the detected language (fastText lid.176)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the fastText `lid.176` confidence (roughly 0-1) for the **top** language guess of each input string -- the companion probability to `detect_lang`.

**When to use:** gate downstream processing on identification quality, e.g. keep only rows the model is sure about with `WHERE nlp.detect_lang_conf(body) > 0.8`.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `FLOAT`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. Edge case: fastText occasionally reports a confidence marginally above 1.0 (e.g. ~1.00001), so do not assert a strict `<= 1.0` upper bound on the result.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang_conf

Returns how confident the fastText `lid.176` model is in the language it picked for each text -- a float near the `[0, 1]` range. A common pattern is to keep only confidently-identified rows by filtering on `nlp.detect_lang_conf(body) > 0.8`.

Use alongside `nlp.detect_lang`. Note the confidence can read slightly above 1.0 for some inputs, so avoid a strict upper-bound assertion.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Confidence of the top language guess for a literal string", "sql": "SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox') AS conf"}]
rows.vgi.title: Detect Language Confidence Score

rows: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox') AS conf
Named entities per text row: (id, ent_text, label, start_char, end_char)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Named-entity recognition as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per detected entity** (people, organizations, places, dates, money, ...) found by the spaCy NER pipeline.

**When to use:** pull structured mentions out of unstructured text -- e.g. every company named across a news corpus, or every date in a contract -- so you can aggregate, filter, or join on them.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key copied onto every emitted row (so you can join entities back to the source); `text :=`, `lang :=`, and `model :=` select the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(ent_text, label, start_char, end_char)` plus the optional id. Text rows with no entities emit nothing; output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# entities

Runs spaCy named-entity recognition over a text column, emitting one row per entity span. Pass the input relation positionally and name the join key with `id :=` so every emitted entity carries the source row's id; `text :=`, `lang :=`, and `model :=` choose the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each output row carries the entity text, its type label (`PERSON`, `ORG`, `GPE`, `DATE`, `MONEY`, ...), and the character span within the source. Rows with no entities produce no output; add an `ORDER BY` for deterministic order.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Explode a literal English document into entities, projecting its key columns", "sql": "SELECT ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' AS body), lang := 'en')"}]

# lemmatize(text, lang, model)

Lemmatizes each text using an explicitly named spaCy model, giving full control over accuracy/speed trade-offs -- for instance naming `en_core_web_sm` for English or a larger `en_core_web_trf` transformer model.

The model must be present in the worker's Python environment. When the `lang` argument is empty the model name alone selects the pipeline.

Normalize text: Unicode NFKC, lowercase, and collapse whitespace

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Canonicalize each text into a comparable form: apply Unicode **NFKC** normalization, casefold (aggressive lowercase), and collapse all runs of whitespace to single spaces (trimming the ends).

**When to use:** before equality joins, deduplication, or grouping on free-text keys so that visually-identical strings differing only in case, full/half-width forms, ligatures, or spacing compare equal.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a normalized `VARCHAR`. NULL input yields NULL. This function is **pure Python** -- no spaCy/fastText model is loaded -- so it is the cheapest function in the worker and always available.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# normalize

Returns a canonical form of each text: Unicode NFKC + casefold + whitespace collapse -- e.g. `  Cafe   DELUXE  ` becomes `cafe deluxe`.

Use it to make free-text keys join and group reliably. Unlike the other cleaners this needs no model, so it runs everywhere with no setup.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Canonicalize a messy literal string for dedup / matching", "sql": "SELECT nlp.main.normalize('  Caf\u00e9   DELUXE\t\u2014  ') AS canonical"}]
rows.vgi.title: Normalize Text Form

rows: SELECT nlp.main.normalize('  Café   DELUXE	—  ') AS canonical
Noun chunks per text row: (id, chunk, root) -- keyword/topic candidates

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Noun-phrase extraction as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per noun chunk** (a base noun phrase such as 'the long road'), each with its head/root token.

**When to use:** mine candidate keywords, topics, or product/feature mentions from free text without training a model -- noun chunks are a cheap, high-recall source of 'what this text is about'.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(chunk, root)` plus the optional id. Text rows with no noun chunks emit nothing; output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# noun_chunks

Extracts base noun phrases from a text column with spaCy, emitting one row per chunk. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every chunk row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row gives the noun-phrase text and its head token (`root`). Aggregate the chunks to surface frequent topics/keywords, or join back to the source via `id :=`.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Explode a literal English document into noun_chunks, projecting its key columns", "sql": "SELECT chunk, root FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT 'The big red car drove down the long road.' AS body), lang := 'en')"}]

Sentences per text row: (id, sent_index, sentence) -- chunking for embeddings

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Sentence segmentation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per sentence**, in document order, with a 0-based index.

**When to use:** chunk long documents into sentence-sized units before embedding/retrieval, sentence-level sentiment, or any per-sentence analysis.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key copied onto every sentence row; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(sent_index, sentence)` plus the optional id. The `sent_index` preserves order; output row order across documents is otherwise not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY id, sent_index` for determinism.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# sentences

Splits a text column into sentences with spaCy, emitting one indexed row per sentence. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every sentence row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row carries the 0-based `sent_index` and the trimmed sentence text. This is the standard first step for sentence-level embeddings or retrieval chunking; use `id :=` to keep sentences tied to their source document, and order by `id, sent_index` for determinism.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Explode a literal English document into sentences, projecting its key columns", "sql": "SELECT sent_index, sentence FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' AS body), lang := 'en')"}]
rows.vgi.result_columns_schema: [{"name": "sent_index", "type": "INTEGER", "description": "0-based index of the sentence within the source text."}, {"name": "sentence", "type": "VARCHAR", "description": "The sentence text."}]

Sentiment score in [-1, 1] (VADER lexicon; tuned for English/social text)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Score the sentiment of each text with VADER and return the **compound** value in `[-1, 1]`, where `-1` is maximally negative, `0` neutral, and `+1` maximally positive.

**When to use:** rank or aggregate opinion in reviews, comments, tweets, and other short social/English text -- e.g. `avg(nlp.sentiment(body))` per product.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `FLOAT` in `[-1, 1]`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. VADER is a lexicon-and-rules model tuned for English and social media; it understands emphasis, negation, and emoticons but is not a translator -- score non-English text only after detecting/translating it.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# sentiment

Returns the VADER compound sentiment score in `[-1, 1]` for each text. A typical use is per-group opinion tracking -- e.g. the average `nlp.sentiment(body)` per product, so you can rank which products reviewers feel best about.

VADER is purpose-built for English social text (handling negation, intensifiers, and emoji). For a coarse neg/neu/pos bucket instead of a number, use `nlp.sentiment_label`.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Score the sentiment of a literal English string", "sql": "SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this, it is fantastic!') AS score"}]
rows.vgi.title: Sentiment Compound Score

rows: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this, it is fantastic!') AS score
Coarse sentiment label: neg / neu / pos (VADER thresholds)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Bucket each text into a coarse three-way sentiment **label** -- `neg`, `neu`, or `pos` -- by thresholding the VADER compound score.

**When to use:** when you want a categorical opinion bucket for `GROUP BY` / filtering rather than a continuous number; cheaper to read in dashboards than the raw score.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` in `{neg, neu, pos}`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. Same English/social-text caveats as `sentiment`; if you need the underlying magnitude, call `nlp.sentiment` instead.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# sentiment_label

Returns a coarse sentiment class -- `neg`, `neu`, or `pos` -- derived from the VADER compound score by thresholding at +/-0.05. A common use is to tally how many reviews fall into each `nlp.sentiment_label(body)` bucket for a dashboard.

Use this when a label is more convenient than the numeric `nlp.sentiment` score, for example to tally how many reviews fall into each mood bucket.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Bucket a literal string into neg / neu / pos", "sql": "SELECT nlp.main.sentiment_label('This is the worst experience ever') AS mood"}]

Languages with a default spaCy pipeline: (lang_code, spacy_model)

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
A **table function** (no arguments) returning one row per language that has a default spaCy pipeline, so the entity/token/sentence/noun-chunk functions and the `lemmatize` / `strip_stopwords` scalars can process it without naming a model.

**When to use:** discover which ISO-639 codes are valid for the `lang` argument before pinning one, or check whether a detected language (from `detect_lang`) has an installed pipeline. Columns: `lang_code` (the ISO-639 value you pass as `lang`) and `spacy_model` (the default small pipeline that backs it).

Note: `detect_lang` recognizes far more languages (fastText covers 176) than have a spaCy pipeline installed -- this table lists only the latter. The named models must also be present in the worker environment to be loadable.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
# supported_languages

Discovery table of every language the worker has a default spaCy pipeline for.

## Columns

- `lang_code` (`VARCHAR`) -- ISO-639 code accepted by the `lang` argument.
- `spacy_model` (`VARCHAR`) -- the default small spaCy model backing it.

Language detection (`detect_lang`) spans 176 languages via fastText, but only the languages listed here can be lemmatized, tokenized, or run through NER without naming a custom model.

rows.vgi.doc_llm:
Tokenization plus linguistic annotation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per token**, each carrying its lemma, part-of-speech, fine-grained tag, stop-word flag, and dependency relation from the spaCy pipeline.

**When to use:** linguistic analysis, building token-level features, counting parts of speech, or filtering to content words -- anything that needs the words of a document as queryable rows.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(token, lemma, pos, tag, is_stop, dep)` plus the optional id. Output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.

# tokens

Tokenizes a text column with spaCy and emits one row per token with rich annotations. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every token row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row gives the token text, its lemma, coarse and fine POS tags, a stop-word flag, and its dependency label. Filter on `is_stop` or `pos` to isolate content words; use `id :=` to join tokens back to their source document.
rows.vgi.example_queries: [{"description": "Explode a literal English document into tokens, projecting its key columns", "sql": "SELECT token, pos FROM nlp.main.tokens((SELECT 'The quick brown fox jumps.' AS body), lang := 'en')"}]
